title: Composition-RL: Compose Your Verifiable Prompts for Reinforcement Learning of Large Language Models
claim: Composing existing problems into harder, verifiable ones before RL training yields better reasoning and cross-domain transfer than training on the original data.
layout: 3 panels: top pipeline left-to-right, bottom line plot and radar chart
description: The top row shows the method on a worked example. Two original math prompts sit on the left, q1 in a blue box and q2 in a green box. Arrows lead to a boxed "Constructed Compositional Prompt" with three steps. Step 1 modifies q1 with its ground truth. Step 2 modifies q2. Step 3 connects them into one yellow merged prompt, with the changes underlined or in red. A final arrow labeled RL Training points to a stylized colorful "Composition-RL" logo. abstract: Large-scale verifiable prompts underpin the success of Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), but they contain many uninformative examples and are costly to expand further. Recent studies focus on better exploiting limited training data by prioritizing hard prompts whose rollout pass rate is 0. However, easy prompts with a pass rate of 1 also become increasingly prevalent as training progresses, thereby reducing the effective data size. To mitigate this, we propose Composition-RL, an offline data-augmentation approach that composes existing prompts before RL to address the pass-rate-1 bottleneck without modifying the RL optimizer. The composed dataset is generated and verified once from the fixed source pool and then used for RL training. Extensive experiments across model sizes from 4B to 30B show that Composition-RL consistently improves reasoning capability over RL trained on the original dataset. Performance can be further boosted with a curriculum variant of Composition-RL that gradually increases compositional depth over training. Additionally, Composition-RL enables more effective cross-domain RL by composing prompts drawn from different domains. All our code, data, and models are publicly available to facilitate future research.
